title: 10 Best UX Design Websites to Learn From in 2026
description: The ten UI/UX design websites worth your time, every link opened and verified in October 2026, with what each one is free for and what it charges.

blocks.v: Most lists of the best UX design websites share one problem: nobody checks the links afterwards. You work through ten recommendations and find three dead domains, two sites that have quietly become something else, and a paywall where the free course used to be.

Every site below was opened and read on 1 October 2026 before it was listed. Where a site has changed since this article was first published, the entry says so. Where something is free, it says what is free and what is not, because "free resource" usually means a free article and a paid course.
These are the ten worth your time, roughly in the order a working designer would actually use them.
The best UX design websites at a glance
How to use a UX design website properly
Reading design websites is not the same as learning design, and it is worth being honest about which one you are doing. Most people who bookmark twenty UX blogs end up reading none of them.

A better approach is to pick one site for each of three jobs. One for research you can cite when somebody questions a decision. One for a structured course if you are learning from scratch. One for a weekly habit, so you see what the field is arguing about. Everything else is reference material you search when a specific problem lands on your desk.
Each entry below says which of those three jobs it does.
1. Nielsen Norman Group

If you only use one site on this list, use this one. Nielsen Norman Group was founded by Jakob Nielsen and Don Norman, and it is the closest thing user experience has to a standards body. When you need to tell a client that their idea will not work, this is where the evidence comes from. The articles are research-backed rather than opinion, which matters enormously in a field where most advice is somebody's preference stated confidently.

v: Best for: settling arguments with evidence
Free: a very large archive of articles, plus a YouTube channel with short research summaries
Paid: training courses and UX certification, priced for companies rather than individuals
Start with: their articles on usability heuristics, which underpin most of the field

blocks.v: 2. Interaction Design Foundation

The largest structured UX education platform online, and the one to use if you want a course rather than a blog. The teaching is organised into proper courses with a beginning and an end, which is exactly what most self-taught designers are missing. It is worth knowing the model before you sign up: the courses run on an annual membership rather than per-course pricing.

v: Best for: learning in a structured order instead of reading at random
Free: a large encyclopedia of UX literature and their design blog
Paid: membership, which unlocks the courses and certificates
Start with: the free encyclopedia chapters before you decide whether to pay

blocks.v: 3. UX Collective

A community publication where working designers write about what they are actually running into. Because it publishes many authors rather than one house voice, the quality varies, but the range is the point: you get accessibility, research methods, design critique and career writing in the same feed. Their newsletter is one of the few in this field worth keeping subscribed to.

v: Best for: a weekly habit, and seeing what practitioners are arguing about
Free: most articles
Note: it is published on Medium, so some articles sit behind Medium's paywall
Start with: the newsletter rather than the site, so it comes to you

blocks.v: 4. Growth.Design

Case studies presented as comics, which sounds gimmicky and is not. Each one walks through a real product decision made by a company you have heard of, then explains the psychology behind why it worked or failed. If you have ever struggled to explain to a client why a change matters, this is the site that teaches you how to tell that story.

v: Best for: understanding the psychology under an interface, and learning to explain it
Free: the case studies
Paid: their courses and premium material
Start with: any case study on a product you already use, so you can check their reasoning against your own experience

blocks.v: 5. Untools

Not a design site at all, which is why it is on the list. Untools is a collection of thinking tools and decision-making frameworks: first principles, second-order thinking, systems maps, and similar. Design problems are usually thinking problems wearing a visual disguise, and this is the site that gives you a structure for the thinking part. Small, free, and completely free of filler.

v: Best for: untangling a problem before you open a design tool
Free: all of it
Start with: the decision-making section

blocks.v: 6. Laws of UX

A single-purpose reference site collecting the psychological principles that come up constantly in interface work: Hick's Law, Fitts's Law, Jakob's Law, the Von Restorff effect, and the rest. Each one gets a plain explanation and the research behind it. This was not in the original version of this article and should have been, because it is the fastest way to put a name to something you already do instinctively.

v: Best for: naming the principle behind a decision you have already made
Free: all of it
Start with: Jakob's Law, which explains most arguments about "making it look different"

blocks.v: 7. Baymard Institute

The most specific site here, and the most valuable if you work on anything that takes payment. Baymard runs large-scale usability research on e-commerce and publishes the findings, including a long-running benchmark of checkout usability across major retailers. If you are designing a cart, a checkout or a product page, this is research you can hand a client directly.

v: Best for: e-commerce, checkout and anything with a conversion target
Free: a substantial portion of their research articles
Paid: full research access and their benchmark database
Start with: their checkout usability findings

blocks.v: 8. UX Hints

Short, specific posts on one idea at a time, organised by topic: accessibility, typography, usability, user testing, UX laws. It still runs the "UX Hints TL;DR" format the name is known for. Useful when you have a narrow question and do not want a 3,000-word essay around the answer.

v: Best for: a quick answer to a specific question
Free: the articles and the newsletter
Start with: the topic index rather than the homepage

blocks.v: 9. Usability Geek

A long-running usability and UX blog with a practical bent. Where Nielsen Norman Group writes the research, Usability Geek tends to write the version you can apply on Monday morning. Strong on accessibility and on the unglamorous parts of usability that get skipped.

v: Best for: practical usability writing you can act on immediately
Free: the blog
Paid: they also list UX courses
Start with: their accessibility writing

blocks.v: 10. Dark Patterns Tip Line

A public archive of deceptive design: the countdown timers that reset, the unsubscribe buttons hidden three screens deep, the pre-ticked boxes. It exists so people can report what has been done to them, which makes it a catalogue of exactly the techniques you should refuse to build. Read it as a list of things to say no to when somebody asks for "something that converts better".

v: Best for: recognising a manipulative pattern before you are asked to build one
Free: all of it
Related: Ethical Design Resources at ethicaldesignresources.com collects the positive version, which is a curated set of tools and references for designing responsibly

blocks.v: One correction from the earlier version of this article

The original list included a site called "Principle.Design" and described it as a prototyping tool for building animated app interfaces. That conflated two different things, and it is worth correcting rather than quietly deleting.

Principle is a Mac prototyping application. principles.design is something else entirely: a free library of real-world design principles published by actual companies and teams, collected as decision-making frameworks. It is a genuinely useful site, it is simply not a prototyping tool. If you were looking for the prototyping application, that is a separate product. If you want the principles library, it is worth a visit for a different reason: reading how other teams wrote their principles is the fastest way to write your own.
More UX websites worth bookmarking
Three more that did not make the ten but earn a place in a browser folder.
Smashing Magazine
Long-form, technically detailed articles sitting at the join between design and front-end code. Particularly good when the problem is a design decision with engineering consequences.
Ethical Design Resources
A curated, maintained collection of tools and references for designing responsibly. Small and still actively updated.
Nielsen Norman Group on YouTube
Listed separately from the main site because the format changes how useful it is. Short videos, usually one research finding each, and easier to get through than the written archive.
Which UX website to start with if you are new

Pick three, not ten. A reasonable starting set is Interaction Design Foundation for structure, Nielsen Norman Group for evidence, and the UX Collective newsletter for a weekly pulse. That covers learning, proving and keeping up.

Then build something. Every site on this list is more useful once you have a real interface in front of you and a specific problem to solve. Reading about usability heuristics in the abstract is far less effective than reading them while looking at a screen you designed and cannot work out why people are abandoning.
Frequently asked questions
What is the difference between UI and UX design?

UX is the decision about what the product does and in what order. UI is the decision about how that looks and behaves on screen. A booking flow that asks for payment before showing the price is a UX problem, and no amount of visual polish fixes it. A booking flow with the right steps but unreadable text is a UI problem. In practice one person often does both, but they fail in different ways and it helps to know which one you are looking at. [[UX designer vs UI designer|/ux-designer-vs-ui-designer]] covers the split in more detail.
Which of these websites is best for a complete beginner?

Interaction Design Foundation, because it is organised as courses rather than as a feed. Beginners usually suffer from too much unordered information rather than too little, and a structured sequence solves that. Laws of UX is a good second, because it gives you vocabulary quickly.
Are any of these actually free?

Untools, Laws of UX and Dark Patterns Tip Line are entirely free. Nielsen Norman Group, Growth.Design, Baymard and Interaction Design Foundation publish a substantial amount free and charge for courses, certification or full research access. UX Collective is free except where an article sits behind Medium's paywall.
What are dark patterns?

Interface designs that work against the person using them: a cancel button hidden behind four screens, a pre-ticked subscription box, a countdown that resets when you reload. They are called deceptive design patterns in current regulatory language. They often do raise short-term conversion, which is why clients ask for them, and they damage trust and increasingly attract regulatory attention. The Dark Patterns Tip Line is a catalogue of them.
Do I need a design degree to work in UI/UX?

No. Portfolios decide hiring in this field, not qualifications. What a portfolio has to show is reasoning rather than screenshots: what the problem was, what you tried, what the result was. Three projects explained properly will beat twenty pretty images. Every site on this list helps you build the reasoning half.
What makes a good user experience website?

Two different things get called a UX website: sites that teach user experience, which is this list, and websites that have good user experience themselves. The second kind share a few traits. The purpose is clear on the first screen, pages load quickly on a phone, text is readable, forms ask only for what is needed, and errors explain how to fix them. Baymard and Nielsen Norman Group both publish research on exactly these points if you want evidence rather than opinion.
How often should I be reading these?

One newsletter weekly, and the rest on demand when a specific problem arrives. Trying to read all ten regularly is how people end up reading none of them. Reference sites are for searching, not for subscribing.
Last checked and updated on 1 October 2026. Every link above was opened and verified on that date.
